articles.title: Two Democrats rescue Mike Johnson's anti-socialism resolution in stunning move
articles.summary: A group of House Republicans threatened to upend Speaker Mike Johnson's plans this week in protest of his handling of federal spending.
articles.body: Two Democrats helped Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., score a commanding victory Tuesday after overcoming a House GOP rebellion to advance a resolution to condemn socialism. House conservatives had threatened to tank a procedural vote, called a "rule vote," meant to unlock debate on several bills GOP leaders wanted lawmakers to vote on this week. That rebellion would have been successful if not for two moderate left-wing lawmakers coming to the GOP's rescue. It's almost unheard of for the minority party to help their political rivals pass a rule. It appears to have blindsided House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who later told reporters he was not notified beforehand. JOHNSON SCORES WIN AS CONSERVATIVE REBELS END HOUSE FLOOR BLOCKADE OVER VOTER ID BILL Five Republicans voted against the rule, which was poised to fail until Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., provided two critical votes to get the GOP over the finish line in a narrow 209 to 208 vote. The five House Republicans who voted against it were Reps. Pete Sessions, R-Texas; Chip Roy, R-Texas; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., Clay Higgins, R-La.; and Andy Harris, R-Md. The rebels' issue was not with the measure itself, nor the bills it would have allowed the House to pass. Their votes were a protest against how their leaders handled a plan to avert a government shutdown just before the midterm elections, a short-term funding bill called a continuing resolution (CR). That measure passed just before the rule vote began. "NO ON CR. NO ON RULE THAT DOES NOT ALLOW US TO AMEND AND FIX THE CR: The House of Representatives will be voting for a government funding continuing resolution TODAY that FAILS to deliver on common-sense policies for the American people," Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, wrote on X. Harris, chair of the House Freedom Caucus, also told reporters he would vote against the rule in protest of the CR. A handful of GOP lawmakers took issue with how the Senate modified an original House-passed CR, including adding an unrelated measure to delay a congressionally approved hemp product ban by 30 days and a provision curbing the Trump administration’s control over federal grants. TENSIONS ERUPT IN HOUSE HEARING AS GOP ADVANCES ANTI-SOCIALISM RESOLUTION WHILE DEMS RAGE: 'SILLY SEASON' "The Senate did violence to our bill," Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "Hemp and the grants are the two big ones … and, frankly, I just don’t think CRs ought to be on suspension. … When you put it on suspension, you’re not asking for my vote, OK. You’re going to get Democrats." Roy also criticized the bill for not cutting off funding to sanctuary jurisdictions or abortion providers like Planned Parenthood. Self wound up voting for the rule, but not the CR. DEMOCRATS BLINK AS SCHUMER HELPS GOP CLEAR KEY SHUTDOWN HURDLE Voting on a bill under "suspension" means it gets fast-tracked past multiple procedural hurdles in exchange for raising the threshold for passage from a simple majority to two-thirds. That means the rule vote's survival does not affect whether the CR passes or fails. A CR is a short-term extension of current federal funding levels. It's normally used to give lawmakers extra time to cobble together a new budget for the next fiscal year, which begins Oct. 1. The CR up for a vote Tuesday would kick the government shutdown fight to a Dec. 11 deadline. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A rule vote traditionally falls along party lines and, until recently, it was unheard of for lawmakers to defy their leaders by joining the other side to defeat it. But it's become increasingly common in recent years for lawmakers, specifically on the right, to weaponize it as a form of protest.

articles.title: Lake Ontario is now Lake America. Residents of Trump-voting Ontario have thoughts.
articles.summary: ONTARIO, N.Y. - Serafino Rosso lives in a big home in this tiny town overlooking the Great Lake it’s named after. When President Donald Trump renamed the lak...
articles.body:
ONTARIO, N.Y. - Serafino Rosso lives in a big home in this tiny town overlooking the Great Lake it's named after. When President Donald Trump renamed the lake, Rosso thought: Why stop there?

"I would like it if they changed the name here to the Town of America: The Town of America on the Lake of America," Rosso, a 41-year-old telecoms manager, said proudly while standing outside Ontario's lone grocery store. "It makes me feel really patriotic. It felt Canadian before."

Trump escalated a trade war with Canada with his executive order renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America, sparking an international outcry. Even in places where most people love Trump, not everyone is on board with upending centuries of tradition to score points in an improvised trade war.

Nowhere is the issue more salient than the place called Ontario on the U.S. side of the lake. Republicans have mixed feelings about the rebrand in this lakefront Upstate New York community of 10,000 in a county that Trump has decisively won in his presidential runs.

"I don't think the lake's name should be changed because it's history," Dave Rupp, who runs the town's liquidation store and voted for Trump in 2024. "And I don't like changing history."

Ontario was originally named Freetown in 1807 in honor of the first settler, Freeman Hopkins. Then it was renamed Ontario less than a year later for the lake forming its northern boundary.

Today, Ontario has seven churches, two Dunkin' restaurants and a town hall. Stickers on pickup trucks read "Respect our farmers."

The influence of agriculture on the town shapes how people view Trump's feud with Canada. Some hope his sweeping tariffs on Canadian goods, including agricultural products, would ultimately help American farmers by easing competition across borders.

The executive order states that the lake's name change is meant "to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements." But while signing the order, Trump told reporters that Canada "has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly." Trump similarly ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed the Gulf of America last year in a dispute over immigration.

Cassandra Tylenda, who voted for Trump, said that she tries to avoid politics, but she hopes that Trump's tariffs help local farmers. Her grandparents had a dairy farm, and she has a small farm where she grows and cans peaches and pickles.

But that doesn't mean she wants to rename the lake.

"I like Lake Ontario better," Tylenda, 29, said while bartending at a local sports bar and restaurant. "But there's nothing I can do about it," she added with a shrug.

The name change has also struck a nerve with the president's detractors.

Rochester Mayor Malik Evans, who leads the heavily Democratic lakefront city west of Ontario, dismissed Trump's executive order as a "publicity stunt."

Serena Eaton, who lives near Ontario, said the renaming was a "distraction" from the Epstein files, the war in Gaza and other issues the Trump administration is facing.

"America doesn't just own the lake," Eaton, 24, said. "I'm not going to call it Lake America. But my town is really redneck. I'm sure a lot of people will just switch their brains off and tune out sensible reason."

Charles Smith, a member of the Cayuga Nation who lives just outside Ontario and has lived in New York and Canada, noted the lake's name has deeper roots far preceding American politics.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney highlighted that same history in response to Trump's order, explaining in an X post that the lake's name comes from "the Wendat word Ontari'io, which, appropriately, means 'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.'"

"It's been Lake Ontario for a very, very long time," Smith, 59, said in an interview outside of one of the two Dunkin' restaurants. "And it will always be Lake Ontario."

The name is already being erased from some official sources. The U.S. Interior Department is updating its geographic systems to reflect Lake America as the new name. Over the weekend, Google Maps changed Lake Ontario's name to Lake America for U.S. users. But Canadians will continue to see the name Lake Ontario.

Some cheered on the revision. After an afternoon riding his boat on the newly christened Lake America, Frankie Amalfi, 33, praised Trump's leadership in taking on what he saw as Canada's unfair trade advantage.

"He will tell you right off the bat that Canada's been getting us for years," Amalfi said as he reclined in Ontario Beach Park's Marina in Rochester. "He doesn't let them walk all over us."

Soaking in the last of the day's sun to the sound of the lapping lake, Amalfi reveled in how the new name annoyed its detractors and referenced a statement made by the president while signing the executive order.

"We have the Gulf of America, the Lake of America," Amalfi said. "All we need now is the Ocean of America."

articles.title: Israel’s multiple wars see finance, defence ministries clash over spending
articles.summary: Spiraling costs of Israel’s conflicts deepen rift between finance and defense ministries ahead of budget decisions.
articles.body:
Israel's Ministries of Finance and Defence have clashed over the spiralling costs of Israel's multiple and ongoing wars in the region, which are adding pressure to the government's budget.

The Israeli military has warned that if the dispute is unresolved it could jeopardise the security of the country.

Since the war on Gaza began in October 2023, Israel has entered its longest period of sustained conflict in its history.

Israeli forces are deployed in Lebanon and Syria as they continue to occupy the Gaza and the West Bank, and are prepared for further conflict with Iran.

Israeli military Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir warned that these costly conflicts are being undertaken with "empty coffers."

The Israeli government has attempted to inject a further 15 billion shekels ($5bn) into the military, the Israeli news website YNet reported, increasing the 2026 defence budget to 184 billion shekels ($60.8bn). The defence funding is a near-record in the country's history, second only to the 188 billion shekels ($62.2bn) spent on defence during the first year of its genocide in Gaza.

Tensions between Israel's defence and finance ministries have been building for some time, with the two sides divided over the scale and management of military spending.

In late August, YNet News reported that the dispute was likely to continue even after the additional funding had been approved.

Senior finance officials rejected the military's claim that it was "on the edge of the abyss" and warned that meeting its demands could push military spending to nearly one-third of the country's entire state budget, the Israeli media outlet added.

"Everything costs money. Their only mode of operation is using military force, as we've seen in Lebanon, Syria, Gaza and Iran, but they never seem to want to talk about paying for it," Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.

"It costs. The hardware, the ammunition, the soldiers, and the benefits if they're injured," he said. "It all needs paying for, which is something they rarely seem to want to discuss."

Complicating the picture is the fragmented nature of Israeli politics, said Makelberg. Politicians compete for small and often uncompromising parts of the electorate that are often unwilling or unable to see beyond their own interests.

That was especially true for Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, whose far-right Religious Zionist Party might not pass the electoral threshold to sit in the next Knesset.

"Smotrich is in an uncomfortable position. On the one hand, he needs the support of these hardcore nationalists who demand more expenditure on the military and their occupation of the West Bank. On the other, as minister of finance, he has to pay for it," he said.

Briefings from within the Israeli military have blamed foot-dragging from the Finance Ministry for a number of potential spending cuts. This includes a sharp reduction in reserve forces in the Northern and Southern Commands, while the West Bank Division will be maintained at current levels despite heightened tensions and security warnings after a wave of settler pogroms against Palestinians in the occupied territory.

The military has also warned that it will significantly scale back intelligence gathering, where operations rely on costly technologies. At the same time, the military has warned that it will need to prepare for a possible escalation with Iran and other threats, including the Houthis in Yemen and pro-Iranian Shia militias in Iraq. All of this will require continuous costly training and adequate stocks of spare parts and munitions.

"Struggling departments often blame the Ministry of Finance for their own problems, much in the way that the government of developing countries sometimes blame the IMF [International Monetary Fund]," said Michael Ben-Gad, a professor of economics at City St George's, University of London said.

"The Ministry of Finance will make sure the army's funded. Most of the people in the ministry have family in the army and/or served themselves."

The political difficulty, especially close to an election, is to be seen to oppose the army.

"Smotrich can either pay now and raise taxes after the election, or pay now and then criticise the next government for doing just that," Ben-Gad said.

Few ministers are showing any appetite to curb Israel's military endeavours, despite the warnings of "empty coffers". In the occupied West Bank, the Israeli army has announced it is preparing a widescale deployment to stem the unrestrained settler violence that many in the government, including Smotrich, have been accused of encouraging.

At the same time, Israel is preparing for an escalation in the conflict with Iran. Billions of dollars are being spent to replenish munition supplies that were expended in both the last war with Iran and Israel's neighbours.

"It's like a rule of nature. Every year, the Israeli army asks for more money and every year the Ministry of Finance will impose a cut of around one to two percent across all other departments to pay for it," Israeli political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg told Al Jazeera.

"We're seeing a fresh military doctrine develop where the Israeli army is establishing front lines in enemy territory, with what they call 'dead zones' behind it," he said.

Not one of the frontrunners in October's election was questioning the wisdom of that tactic.

"If this is the new doctrine, then it could be an expensive one, as those frontlines are going to need to be replenished with both manpower and equipment," Flaschenberg said.

"There might be disagreements over how that capacity is eventually deployed, but not the doctrine of building it up."

articles.title: Kremlin: Germany taking path of escalation over Leipzig drone affair
articles.summary: The Kremlin has accused Germany of pursuing a course of escalation following threats of sanctions over the unexploded explosive drone found at Leipzig airpor...
articles.body:
The Kremlin has accused Germany of pursuing a course of escalation following threats of sanctions over the unexploded explosive drone found at Leipzig airport.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday evening that it was difficult to comment on the accusations against Russia because Germany had provided no evidence for its allegations: "When such serious accusations are made, they should be substantiated in some way," Peskov said, according to the Russian news agency Interfax.

The close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin also accused Germany of failing to back up its allegations with arguments. "It is obvious that Germany is taking the further path of escalation," Peskov said, adding that Russia had consistently denied any involvement with the Leipzig drone.

Moscow instead pointed to Kiev, which it said was benefiting from stirring up sentiment against Russia over the hybrid attack.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul held Russia responsible for the drone incident and announced punitive measures earlier on Tuesday evening. Wadephul said the Russian consulate in Bonn would be closed and the contract for the Russian House cultural institute in Berlin would be terminated.

Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told dpa that Moscow would impose counter-sanctions, as in previous cases.

In a post on Telegram, Zakharova asked - with reference to the anniversary of Germany's launch of World War II - whether the government in Berlin had chosen the date by chance.

Parts of the Moscow leadership have repeatedly referred to Chancellor Friedrich Merz as "Fritz," a derogatory term for Germans.

Germany started World War II on September 1, 1939, and subsequently invaded the Soviet Union.

articles.title: Milo Yiannopoulos ‘very ashamed’ of support for Trump after deportation
articles.summary: Far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos said he is “very ashamed” for supporting President Trump after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detained and deported him back to the United Kingdom. Yiannopoulos told British commentator Piers Morgan on his talk show “Uncensored” on YouTube that he believes the Trump administration has “devolved into the Loomer admin,” referring to…
articles.body:
Far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos said he is “very ashamed” for supporting President Trump after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detained and deported him back to the United Kingdom.

Yiannopoulos told British commentator Piers Morgan on his talk show “Uncensored” on YouTube that he believes the Trump administration has “devolved into the Loomer admin,” referring to far-right influencer Laura Loomer, who took credit for reporting Yiannopoulos to ICE.

“To think that the promise and hope and joy and anticipation of Trump 2016 could, over the course of 10 years, collapse into this ugly, war-mongering –– taken as a whole, mentally ill heap of crazy with some of the most unstable and lunatic people seemingly directing the president’s actions,” Yiannopoulos told Morgan.

“If,” he added, “I had any clue that anything remotely like this was even possible, I would never have gotten involved in supporting Trump in the first place. And I’m very ashamed that I did.”

ICE detained Yiannopoulos, a vocal critic of immigrants in the country illegally and supporter of Trump’s deportation agenda, Thursday night at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport (MSY) in Kenner, La., ahead of a Friday concert for Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, in New Orleans, TMZ reported.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) deported the British national back to his home country on Friday. Federal officials said he legally entered the U.S. on May 14 and was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on July 22 when he did not appear at an immigration hearing.

The usually colorful and provocative Yiannopoulos spoke on “Uncensored” in a lowered tone in describing his thoughts on Trump, Loomer and his deportation.

Yiannopoulos described the process of being detained, calling it “humiliating and disorienting.” He said he experienced “brutality” as he passed through the immigration system.

“It was physically degrading, it was frightening,” he said. “I don’t think I’ve ever been frightened like that before … And I was weeping like an old woman for an hour. And I was like, ‘Oh, I really have got to get this out of my system.'”

He reflected on being “a little bit blasé” and “cavalier” about when people shared their traumas, saying that he now understands it.

“I wouldn’t wish it on anyone,” Yiannopoulos added.

He dismissed White House border czar Tom Homan’s remarks about Yiannopoulos overstaying his visa. Yiannopoulos said he did no such thing and that he is married to an American. He said he had an O-1 visa, a nonimmigrant work permit for individuals with “extraordinary ability,” as the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services describes it .

He said he filed for an adjustment to his status from a visa to a green card but never received any notices for a hearing, saying they went to an old address.

Yiannopoulos also shared some of his history with Loomer, telling Morgan that he worked on her failed 2020 House campaign in Florida. He said he was positioned to work as her communications director until it appeared that “there was something very, very wrong with her.”

He described her relationship with Trump as “symbiotic” and said the president “lets her run riot.” Morgan interjected to prevent Yiannopoulos from sharing further details, citing U.K. defamation law.

Yiannopoulos built his reputation as a conservative firebrand in his writing for the far-right Breitbart News, which published his incendiary comments about Muslims, women and other groups of people. He stepped down in 2017 from his role as senior editor at Breitbart after he made comments that appeared to condone pedophilia. He later apologized.

articles.body:
A Haitian-born student in Ohio reportedly took his own life following the loss of his immigration status as part of the Trump administration’s termination of temporary protected status for immigrants around the country.

The Ohio State Highway Patrol stated in a Monday press release that 20-year-old Pierre Damas Bel died Monday when he walked into oncoming traffic after he parked his vehicle on the right shoulder of Interstate 70.

“Bel succumbed to fatal injuries at the scene,” Ohio State Highway Patrol stated.

The agency reported this was an open investigation and declined to give additional details.

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) said Tuesday that Bel’s death is a “horrible, horrible tragedy.”

“I think we have to ask ourselves: Is this really good? Is it what we want done to people like this being picked up and facing deportation? Do we want that being done in our name,” he added.

Bel was reportedly “distraught” after weeks wearing an ankle monitor, according to remarks his father made to The Haitian Times . He was one of the many Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, who were ordered by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to begin wearing ankle monitors.

“In his last days, I did not recognize him as he was such an energetic kid who loves life, friends and family, and education,” Bel’s father, Pierre Ronal Bel, said in Haitian Creole.

A month before his death, Bel wrote on social media about his experience wearing the ankle monitor, saying, “I came to this country to pursue my education. I didn’t come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone.”

“Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience,” he wrote. “I came here to study, to build my future and to live a better [life,] not to be treated like a criminal. So now, how am I supposed to play college sports with a GPS monitor on my leg?”

ICE declined to comment on Bel’s cause of death and said it “will not speculate about unverified claims regarding other individuals,” according to a statement obtained by NBC affiliate WBTN .

The 20-year-old was previously covered under temporary protected status, a U.S. program that protects people from deportation. It covers foreign nationals who cannot safely return to their home country and offers them a pathway to work authorization.

The Supreme Court ruled in June that the Trump administration could end the protection for the around 330,000 Haitians and more than 6,000 Syrians covered by the program.

This comes as the U.S. still has a ban on flights in and out of Haiti’s main airport due to ongoing gang violence. The State Department also still lists Haiti as a “ Level 4: Do Not Travel ” country on its travel advisory website — citing terrorism, unrest and limited healthcare services in the nation.

Announcing his decision to step down as CEO in April, Apple said Cook will “assist with certain aspects of the company” as executive chair, including “engaging with policymakers around the world.”

Specifically, Cook told Ternus he will manage Apple’s relationships with President Trump and the Chinese government, Bloomberg reported .

articles.body:
A specialized Border Patrol team is joining the search for a hiker still missing in the Grand Canyon after a flash flood killed at least two people and forced the evacuation of dozens over the weekend.

John Guisti, 46, and Brent Rosenkranz, 42, were both killed in the flooding, their families confirmed Tuesday. They had arrived at the Grand Canyon on Friday to hike and fish with a third friend, Timothy Smith, 53, who still remains unaccounted for.

A Border Patrol technical search team will be deployed to assist National Park Service crews as they search during another round of potentially dangerous weather.

Heavy rain and thunderstorms could bring additional flash flooding, along with debris flows and rock falls, complicating efforts to search the canyon.

Authorities also plan to use a drone from the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office that can scan for Bluetooth signals from electronic devices, according to reports .

Rangers have used information such as camping permits and license plates to account for people who may have been in the area when the flooding began. Officials said Monday that they had no indication that anyone other than Smith remained missing.

Nearly 80 people have been rescued since Saturday’s floods, including visitors trapped at a lodge near the bottom of the canyon that is only accessible by foot or along the Colorado River.

Several rounds of rainfall had already left creeks running before another wave of storms triggered the flooding, according to the National Weather Service. Flash floods are a known hazard in the Grand Canyon during Arizona’s summer monsoon season, when thunderstorms can bring heavy rain to the steep terrain with little warning.

Rain also fell over part of the burn scar left by the Dragon Bravo wildfire, which burned more than 227 square miles last year. Burned areas have an increased risk of flash flooding because vegetation that would normally slow runoff was destroyed in the fires.

articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Administration details oil deal with Venezuela The Trump administration unveiled additional details Monday evening about its new oil deal with Venezuela. articles.body:
Administration details oil deal with Venezuela

The Trump administration unveiled additional details Monday evening about its new oil deal with Venezuela.

The administration said in a press release that the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital will take a 35 percent equity stake in North American Blue Energy Partners, a private company that is Venezuela’s second-largest private oil producer.

It added that the firm, which will now be partly owned by the U.S. government, was given a 100-year concession for Venezuelan oil fields that are estimated to contain about 65 billion barrels of oil — about 21 percent of Venezuela’s total estimated oil.

The administration also said that the U.S. will get the right to purchase 20 percent of the oil that North American Blue Energy Partners unearths at the cost of production.

It said that this oil can be used to fill the U.S.’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which both the Trump and Biden administrations have pulled from in recent years to mitigate the fuel price impacts of the war in Iran and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

The State Department will also be given the first right of refusal to purchase the other 80 percent of the oil the company produces.

The administration said that “millions of barrels” produced in Venezuela will be processed by U.S. refineries, but it did not specify a number or percentage.

articles.title: Ohio man pleads guilty to smashing windows at Vance’s home
articles.summary: An Ohio man pleaded guilty Tuesday to vandalizing Vice President JD Vance’s Cincinnati home earlier this year. William D. DeFoor pleaded guilty in federal court to engaging in acts of physical violence against government officials or property and causing willful injury or depredation to property of the U.S., Justice Department (DOJ) officials said in a…
articles.body:
An Ohio man pleaded guilty Tuesday to vandalizing Vice President JD Vance’s Cincinnati home earlier this year.

William D. DeFoor pleaded guilty in federal court to engaging in acts of physical violence against government officials or property and causing willful injury or depredation to property of the U.S., Justice Department (DOJ) officials said in a release .

The charges stemmed from DeFoor’s Jan. 5 attack on the Vance family’s home. At around midnight that day, Secret Service officers observed the 26-year-old running along the front fence of the residence, the DOJ noted Tuesday.

The man then breached the property line at the driveway, struck the driver’s side window of an unmarked federal law enforcement vehicle blocking the driveway three times with a hammer and broke the glass windows at the front of the residence, per the department.

Federal prosecutors said DeFoor’s strikes on the “enhanced security assets” on each window owned by the federal government caused $28,000 in damages.

The Secret Service took DeFoor into custody shortly after the incident in January. Vance and his family were in Washington, D.C., when DeFoor carried out the attack.

The vice president and Second Lady Usha Vance have four children, with Usha Vance giving birth to the couple’s youngest in July.

Vance said at the time a “crazy person” tried to break into the home by “hammering the windows.”

The vice president added he was “grateful” to Secret Service and Cincinnati Police Department officers for “responding so quickly” to the incident.”

U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Ohio Dominick S. Gerace II, whose office prosecuted the case, said acts of violence “directed against our political leaders, their families, or property, have no place” in society.

“Our elected leaders, at all levels of government, must be permitted to carry out their duties free from threats, vandalism, and other forms of violence,” Gerace added in Tuesday’s release. “Perpetrators like DeFoor, who put that freedom at risk, particularly through violent, destructive actions, will, like here, be vigorously prosecuted.”

DeFoor faces up to 20 years in prison, 10 years for each count he pleaded guilty. U.S. District Judge Douglas R. Cole, an appointee of President Trump, will determine the man’s sentence.

DeFoor has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and his attorney has previously said his client’s actions were not political, WKRC-TV in Cincinnati reported Tuesday .

DeFoor’s mother, Catherine DeFoor, said in January that mental illness “has taken over” her child’s life “in a way that we could never have imagined,” according to WKRC-TV .

articles.body:
The man accused of bringing a guillotine near the United States Capitol Building reportedly posted his plans on social media before traveling to the nation’s capital.

Philan-Tam-Duy Le posted on social platform Instagram a video on Aug. 12 showing a guillotine and appeared to be wearing an executioner’s hood in parts of the video. He stated that he was growing frustrated with lawmakers and defense contractors for “getting us involved in international conflicts and forever wars.”

He said that he has “been working on a solution” for his grievances before showing the guillotine in the truck bed of a black truck – claiming it is “strictly for self-defense purposes.”

“I want to make things very clear: I harbor no ill will or intentions of violence toward anyone, religiously, politically, scientifically, financially, musically or socioeconomically,” he added.

“SAN DIEGO TO THE CAPITAL MOTHERF- – – ERS LATER,” he concluded in the video’s caption.

Le – a tattoo artist in Julian, Calif. located about 60 miles northeast of San Diego – is currently facing one count of carrying a dangerous weapon for his alleged actions.

U.S. Capitol Police officers Sergei Vittone, Ryerson Hill and Joseph Diaz – according to an affidavit to the Superior Court of the District of Columbia – were the first to spot an illegally parked black Toyota Tacoma with a guillotine in the truck bed.

Hill confirmed that the guillotine was real after tapping on the blade section of it.

During questioning by Vittone and Hill before he was arrested , Le told the officers he was not near the Capitol “for any specific reason” and “didn’t have issues with specific members of Congress,” according to the affidavit.

In a Saturday post , Le confirmed he had been released from prison on Aug. 26 and will stand for trial on Sep. 24. He also declined to comment further on ongoing investigations.

articles.title: Republicans turn on House GOP lawmaker accused of late-night texts, lavish gifts to female staffers
articles.summary: Several House Republicans joined Democrats to censure Chuck Edwards after an ethics probe found he created a hostile work environment for staffers.
articles.body: Nearly every House Republican joined all Democrats to admonish one of their own after a bombshell investigation found that the lawmaker had engaged in "unprofessional and inappropriate conduct" with his staff. The House voted to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., on a landslide 413 to 2 vote as Congress has grappled with multiple incidents of alleged sexual harassment and misconduct by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. Only Edwards and Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., voted against the resolution. The censure vote on Tuesday comes on the heels of a bombshell House Ethics Committee report released last month that recommended Edwards be rebuked for "persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers." BAD BOSSES ON CAPITOL HILL COULD FACE RECKONING UNDER NEW ANONYMOUS STAFFER REVIEW PLATFORM The committee is chaired by Edwards' fellow Republican Rep. Michael Guest, R-Miss., but acts on a bipartisan basis to investigate lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. Guest noted on the House floor that the investigation did not find evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity, nor did he explicitly proposition the staffers, but that his "conduct toward two young female staffers was inappropriate and violated rules prohibiting sexual harassment," and that it created a hostile work environment. "The committee found that Representative Edwards was, at a minimum, blind to the reality and at worst dismissive of the impact his conduct had on the career and well-being of the women on his staff," Guest said. REPLACEMENT GOP NOMINEE NAMED AFTER REP CHUCK EDWARDS DROPS RE-ELECTION BID Ahead of the vote, Edwards told Fox News Digital, "They’ll make their argument, and I’ll make mine," and countered that the House Ethics Committee had abandoned "its own rules" in its handling of his case. That report detailed lavish gifts, trips, and the reading of a poem to one of the staffers, going to a staffer's home to perform chores, late-night personal texts, and taking one of the staffers to a casino, among other interactions. He ended his bid for re-election two days after its release. He disputed the report on the House floor — after apologizing to the pair of staffers at the center of the Ethics Committee’s probe, along with his wife and family — accusing the bipartisan panel of cherry-picking the context of the incidents to fit a specific narrative. He challenged the censure vote at hand and contended that his regret over the situation was "not an admission of sexual harassment." "Generosity is not sexual harassment. Caring deeply about the people with whom you've worked for years is not sexual harassment," Edwards said. "And conduct that is otherwise permissible does not automatically become misconduct, simply because enough individual moments are assembled together and viewed through the darkest possible ends." CAPITOL SEX SCANDALS SPARK PUSH TO BAN HOUSE LAWMAKERS FROM SLEEPING WITH STAFFERS Still, his arguments weren’t enough to dissuade his colleagues. Notably, the entirety of House Republican leadership voted for the resolution. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., who chairs the Democratic Women’s Caucus, contended that since Edwards "continues to show no remorse, it's obvious that Edwards refuses to understand sexual harassment or his abuse of power." "If we don't take action today, there is no opportunity for these women to receive justice," Leger Fernández said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Edwards became the 30th member of the House of Representatives to be censured, which carries the penalty of a public rebuke for his conduct but does not force him to resign from his seat. It also comes as other members of the House have grappled with their colleagues’ conduct in recent months. Earlier this year, former Reps. Eric Swalwell and Tony Gonzales both resigned on the same day. Swalwell resigned after being hit with allegations of rape and sexual assault, while Gonzales exited Congress after being accused of sexual misconduct with a former staffer, and after he admitted to having an affair with his former staffer, Regina Santos-Aviles, who later died by setting herself on fire. Both faced the rare threat of expulsion.

articles.title: House censures GOP Rep. Chuck Edwards over ‘inappropriate conduct’ with female staffers
articles.summary: A bipartisan ethics probe found Edwards, R-N.C., showered the aides with lavish gifts, invited them to intimate dinners and trips and wrote them poetry. He denied any wrongdoing.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The House overwhelmingly voted Tuesday to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., after a monthslong ethics investigation found that he “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.” The vote was 413-2, with the only no votes coming from Edwards himself and Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C. A simple majority was needed to pass the censure resolution. The resolution is a formal rebuke of Edwards, who is in his second term, but does not force him out of office. After the vote, Edwards was required to stand in the well of the House chamber, before his colleagues, as Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., read the resolution aloud. Edwards, 65, had unequivocally rejected the Ethics Committee’s findings, but he did end his re-election campaign after the committee recommended censuring him. A panel of GOP leaders in North Carolina later picked GOP state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to replace him on the November ballot. The bipartisan House Ethics Committee issued a 25-page report last month detailing multiple incidents of bizarre behavior, “poor judgment and unbecoming conduct” by Edwards. The committee found that Edwards, who is married, provided two young women who worked for him with lavish, high-value gifts, including jewelry, designer purses, handguns and tickets to the musical “Hamilton”; frequently commented on their appearance and dress; invited them to intimate dinners and vacations; and sent notes about his “effusive affection.” On one occasion, the committee found, Edwards went to the home of one of the women, known as Staffer 2, and helped decorate her Christmas tree; he skipped votes that day to do so, he told her. He also wrote poems for Staffer 2, one of which he read at her going-away party in his office, where he cried. Other staffers later testified it made them feel uncomfortable. The committee did not find any evidence that Edwards “engaged in sexual activity with or explicitly propositioned any individual under his employ,” according to the report. However, it added, “Representative Edwards was at minimum blind to that reality, and at worst, dismissive of the impact his inappropriate conduct had on the careers and wellbeing of two women on his staff.” Last week, Edwards reportedly sent a 22-page letter to colleagues defending his actions and arguing that nothing found by the ethics probe could be construed as “sexual misconduct.” “An affectionate friendship is not a sexual proposition. A gift is not sexual misconduct. A compliment is not sexual misconduct. Poetry is not sexual misconduct. Socializing with a colleague is not sexual misconduct. Caring deeply about someone with whom you have worked and come to know for years is not sexual misconduct,” he wrote. “Yet individual acts that were not themselves prohibited were gathered together, assigned the most damaging possible interpretation, and then used collectively to support a conclusion far more serious than the underlying evidence.” Edwards pointed out that the Ethics Committee in its own report said it had found no evidence that he engaged in sexual activity with or propositioned any of his staffers. And he noted that the committee said the allegations “do not implicate quid pro quo sexual harassment” or violate “the ‘letter’ of federal sexual harassment law.” However, the bipartisan panel — led by Chairman Michael Guest, R-Miss., and ranking member Mark DeSalnier, D-Calif. — said Edwards’ behavior with female staffers and former staffers violated the House Code of Official Conduct by failing to adhere to the “spirit of rules” barring sexual harassment and unwanted advances to staff members. In other examples detailed by the committee, Edwards planned elaborate outings with the two young women. He took Staffer 1 on a political trip to New York City, and they stayed for an extra day for his birthday. He sought to “surprise” her that day, the committee said, with a helicopter ride, dinner and a Broadway show. On a different occasion, Edwards suggested to Staffer 2 that they could go to Annapolis, Maryland, “for lunch, meditate by its water, stroll about town, find a day spa, see a movie, or wipe out the casino,” according to the panel’s report. And text messages obtained by the committee show that Edwards sent roughly 30 different types of ice cream to Staffer 2’s home to try to cheer her up. “Thank you, but this seems a bit excessive,” she texted him. In his letter to colleagues, Edwards argued that he had a long-standing relationship with those two staffers, dating to his North Carolina state Senate office and “grueling campaigns.” He also said he gave personal gifts to other staffers in his office, men and women alike. Speaking on the House floor before the vote, Edwards apologized to his wife and family. He also apologized to the two staffers: “I’m sorry that my actions, my judgment or the way that I expressed a friendship ever put either of you in an uncomfortable position.” But he added, “Regret is not an admission of sexual harassment.” “I can acknowledge poor judgment, regret the discomfort that some of my actions may have caused and apologize to those who were hurt by this episode,” he said, “while still disputing a conclusion that the evidence just simply does not support.”

articles.title: House censures North Carolina Republican over allegations of inappropriate behavior with staffers
articles.summary: House lawmakers in both parties came together on Tuesday to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) over allegations of inappropriate behavior with female staffers in his office, marking the latest in a string of disciplinary actions against sitting lawmakers this Congress. The vote was 413-2, fueled by a damning Ethics Committee report, released early last month,…
articles.body:
House lawmakers in both parties came together on Tuesday to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) over allegations of inappropriate behavior with female staffers in his office, marking the latest in a string of disciplinary actions against sitting lawmakers this Congress.

The vote was 413-2, fueled by a damning Ethics Committee report, released early last month, which found that Edwards had demonstrated “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.”

That conduct included a series of expensive gifts, extensive travel, and public comments about their appearance.

The committee determined Edwards violated “the spirit” of the chamber’s rules against sexual harassment and unwanted advances and recommended he be censured .

Edwards dropped his bid for reelection in November, shortly after the report was released. But he has since defended his actions, arguing that the Ethics panel cherrypicked specific episodes to fit a narrative. He continued that defense on Tuesday afternoon on the House floor, where he apologized to the staffers but also insisted that his behavior was not egregious enough to merit censure.

“Regret is not an admission of sexual harassment,” Edwards said. “I can acknowledge poor judgment, regret the discomfort that some of my actions may have caused and apologize to those who were hurt by this episode while still disputing a conclusion that the evidence simply does not support.”

Edwards’s colleagues disagreed, voting overwhelmingly to censure him shortly afterwards. He is the 29th lawmaker to ever be censured by the House.

It marked just the most recent scandal facing a House lawmaker this Congress, spurring calls to reform how the Ethics Commitee and the House more broadly treats allegations of sexual misconduct, harassment and other claims.

In April, Reps. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.) and Tony Gonzales (R-Texas) both resigned in the face of expulsion votes after being accused of sexual misconduct with staffers, with Swalwell also facing an accusation of sexual assault, which he denied.

The Ethics Committee has also opened investigations into Reps. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.), Cory Mills (R-Fla.) and Max Miller (R-Ohio) involving allegations of sexual harassment, dating violence or domestic abuse, respectively. Mills lost his Florida primary earlier this month while Miller has vowed to remain in his race. All three have denied wrongdoing.

Lawmakers have also faced discipline for other reasons. Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (D-Fla.) resigned abruptly while facing accusations of criminal financial fraud. And in early 2025, the House censured Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) for heckling President Trump during the first joint address to Congress of the president’s second term.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy’s jury is deadlocked. What happens if there’s a hung jury?
articles.summary: Judge William Sullivan urged the jury to continue reviewing the facts of the case and sent them back to deliberate.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The jury in the Lindsay Clancy trial informed the judge Tuesday it was deadlocked and unable to reach a unanimous decision.

Judge William Sullivan urged the jury to continue reviewing the facts of the case and sent them back to deliberate.

Clancy is charged with three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan Clancy in the basement of the family’s home in Duxbury, Massachusetts.

Here’s what can happen if the jury is unable to reach a verdict.

Prosecutors have the option of retrying in front of a different jury in a new trial.

She strangled the kids with exercise bands, then tried to take her own life by jumping from a second-story window, an attempt her attorneys say left her paralyzed from the waist down. Her defense argues she was in postpartum psychosis and should not be criminally responsible for the deaths.

Under Massachusetts law , a defendant is not guilty if they lacked criminal responsibility when they committed the offense.

Prosecutors had the burden to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy did not have a mental disease or defect at the time of the crime, or that, even if she did, she “retained the substantial capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness or criminality of (her) conduct and to conform (her) conduct to the requirements of the law.”

Twelve jurors —nine women and three men — are deliberating the case following Clancy’s trial.

If they cannot reach a unanimous decision, the foreperson alerts the judge that the jury is deadlocked.

The judge has the legal authority to keep the jurors deliberating.

If the jury foreperson returns again to alert the judge they are still deadlocked, it’s up to the judge to decide whether they have spent enough time deliberating before declaring a mistrial.

The trial is over, but the prosecution then determines whether the case will be retried. They can also negotiate a plea deal with the defendant.

Karen Read’s first Massachusetts trial ended in hung jury

Karen Read was recently tried for murder in Massachusetts in a case that ended in a hung jury, before she was eventually found not guilty in her following trial. The jury deliberated for 20 hours after her first trial.

Read, 46, was accused of striking her boyfriend, Boston Police Officer John O’Keefe, with her car and leaving him to die in a snowstorm in January 2022. She has maintained her innocence, suggesting she was framed and alleging a cover-up by law enforcement.

She was charged with second-degree murder, manslaughter while operating a vehicle under the influence and leaving the scene.

articles.title: US House passes funding bill to avert government shutdown ahead of midterms
articles.summary: The temporary measure gives Congress until December to fully fund the federal government for fiscal year 2027.
articles.body:
The United States House of Representatives has approved a temporary spending measure that will keep the federal government funded through December 11.

The measure passed by a vote of 370 to 48 on Tuesday after clearing the Senate on August 8. It now goes to President Donald Trump for his signature.

Prior to Tuesday’s stopgap measure, existing government funding was set to expire on October 1, after the new fiscal year begins.

Normally, Congress must pass 12 spending bills to fully fund the federal government’s programmes. Those spending bills are divided into categories such as homeland security, energy, housing and defence.

But Congress has yet to finish such bills for the 2027 fiscal year, which runs through September 30, 2027.

The stopgap measure, known as a continuing resolution, allows lawmakers more time to negotiate the full-year spending bills.

The vote also removes the immediate threat of another government shutdown as lawmakers prepare for the midterm elections on November 3. The elections will decide which party controls each of Congress’s two chambers — a factor that could shape upcoming budget negotiations.

Government shutdowns are widely unpopular in the US. If one were to happen before an election, political analysts speculate it would dampen the chances of re-election for sitting lawmakers.

“This will give Congress time to get past the November elections,” Republican House Appropriations Committee Chairman Tom Cole said during debate, in a seeming acknowledgement of the voting-season predicament.

Democrats have been embroiled in fights with Republicans, who hold the majority in both legislative chambers , since the start of Trump’s second term.

Those disputes have resulted in three government shutdowns , lasting a combined 161 days.

The first came in October 2025, with the extension of healthcare subsides serving as a primary sticking point between the two parties. At 43 days, it was the longest-ever government shutdown in US history.

Afterwards, a partial shutdown took place in January, lasting roughly four days. But several weeks later, a third shutdown occurred targeting the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

The third shutdown came after the deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, who were shot by immigration agents in Minnesota. Democrats tried to withhold funding from the department to advance reforms to agencies under DHS control, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Critics have called such shutdowns ineffective in pushing forward policy change.

Many analysts have also noted that the Trump administration has used the shutdowns to justify unilateral cuts to federal spending and staffing.

Democratic Representative Rosa DeLauro argued that Tuesday’s stopgap bill would allow Congress to reclaim its constitutional authority over government spending.

“The power of the purse resides within the Congress. It is our exclusive responsibility,” DeLauro said, adding, “The first step in exercising that authority is passing this bill today.”

The temporary measure does not address the country’s broader fiscal challenges. The US national debt crossed $40 trillion last month, while affordability remains a major concern for voters.

With Congress delaying decisions on spending priorities for another 15 weeks, lawmakers will also face a tighter timeline in December to write and pass the full-year spending bills.

articles.title: Vulnerable Democrats vote to denounce socialism amid midterm pressure
articles.summary: Several Democratic lawmakers in the House of Representatives voted with Republicans to adopt a resolution that formally denounces socialism and the Democratic Socialists of America. The move reflects increasing pressure on Democrats to respond to the successes of DSA-backed candidates in primaries around the country as Republicans look to make anti-socialism a winning message. Reps.…
articles.body:
Several Democratic lawmakers in the House of Representatives voted with Republicans to adopt a resolution that formally denounces socialism and the Democratic Socialists of America. The move reflects increasing pressure on Democrats to respond to the successes of DSA-backed candidates in primaries around the country as Republicans look to make anti-socialism a winning message.

Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine), Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.), Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), Henry Cuellar (D-Texas), Don Davis (D-N.C.), Darren Soto (D-Fla.), and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) all voted for the resolution denouncing socialism, bucking Democratic leadership. Reps. Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pa.) and Maggie Goodlander (D-N.H.) voted present.

All eight “yes” votes are in competitive races for their seat this year. Six of those races are rated as “toss-up” or “lean Republican” by the Cook Political Report. Two, Vasquez and Cuellar, are rated “lean Democrat,” which still indicates a challenging race.

Democrats are increasingly having to defend their party from Republican attacks as the DSA has gained ground in primaries throughout the year. Republicans are staking out a battleground as defenders of capitalism while condemning socialism , and the House resolution was a chance to put Democrats on the record opting not to denounce socialism.

But the resolution also contained a measure calling for passage of the SAVE America Act, President Trump’s top-priority voter identification bill. That bill has passed the House on party lines and failed the Senate multiple times, but Republicans insist that condemning socialism goes hand in hand with fixing what they see as problems with election security.

Including a statement of support for the voter ID bill in the resolution, even if nonbinding, was guaranteed to cement many Democrats against it. That bill would require proof of citizenship to register to vote and photo ID to vote.

The Democrats who voted for it anyway said they did so because they saw anxiety about socialism from their constituents and wanted to make a statement.

“Back home in Florida right now, folks are very concerned with the rise of socialism,” Castor told The Hill after the vote. “It comes mainly from the Cuban and Venezuelan folks. They watch what’s happened to their communities when you have that kind of government, and it’s really a tip of the hat to them and their concerns.”

As for the voter ID provision attached, Castor didn’t sweat it because, she said, this was just a signal because the bill cannot pass Congress.

“That’s a joke,” she said of the SAVE provision. “And thankfully, that’s not going anywhere.”

Gonzalez told reporters after the vote that he generally opposes socialism and supports voter ID, although he doesn’t want the provisions in SAVE, like limits to mail-in voting, to come at the expense of older adults and other groups.

“Socialism, I don’t know, I’m from the ’80s. Socialism was not a good word for us, right?” Gonzalez said. “And it just never worked. And I think that most Americans don’t agree with some of those proposals.”

“I’ve always been for voter ID,” Gonzalez added. “We can’t vote in France, and the French can’t vote here, and I think that’s a standard rule across the world.”

Gonzalez said he told leadership he would vote no in advance, as he always does.

“We’re just straight talking people, we tell you what we’re going to do and we do what we say we’re going to do,” Gonzalez said.

When asked if leadership pushed back at all, he brushed it off.

“I get a lot of pushback all the time,” he said.

Gluesenkamp Perez, who is one of the Democratic members most likely to vote with Republicans, posted on social media after the vote, appearing to criticize the SAVE portion while acknowledging the socialism issue is far from a top priority for Americas.

“Working America is hanging on by a thread, trying to feed our families without being beholden to big government or big business,” Gluesenkamp Perez wrote. “Standing around pointing fingers, debating -isms and making people photocopy their birth certificate every time they cast a ballot is not the job.”

articles.title: Georgia officer shoots, kills baby donkey ‘HeeHaw’ during missing child search
articles.summary: The Georgia Department of Agriculture is investigating the circumstances surrounding that was shot by an officer.
articles.body:
GEORGIA ( WRBL ) — The Georgia Department of Agriculture is investigating the circumstances surrounding the death of a baby donkey that was shot in Polk County early Sunday morning.

According to the Cedartown Police Department, an officer was searching for a child who was reported missing on Saturday. The child was later found at a nearby church.

“During that search, it is with heavy heart that I report a Cedartown police officer shot and killed a donkey that was in its own pasture,” said Chief Jamie Newsome in a video posted to Facebook . “I cannot imagine the grief and frustration that the tragic loss of HeeHaw has caused.”

The donkey’s owner, Hannah Israel, posted about HeeHaw’s death on social media, alleging the officers entered the pasture “WITHOUT permission or warning.”

“They claimed he ran up to them braying and they thought they were in danger and shot and killed him after trying to taze him,” Israel wrote.

“He was a loved member of our family and did many petting zoos and made many people smile,” she added on GoFundMe.

Newsome said the Georgia Department of Agriculture’s Law Enforcement division is conducting an independent investigation into the shooting. Due to the nature of the investigation, neither the Cedartown Police Department nor the Polk County Police Department could comment further on the case.

The officer responsible for the shooting has been placed on paid administrative leave, pending the investigation’s results, the police chief said.

“I ask everyone to join us in prayer for everyone who has been impacted by this tragic event, but give time for the investigation to be completed,” Newsome said.

articles.title: House passes postponement on hemp ban
articles.summary: Click in for more news from The Hill {beacon} Healthcare The Big Story House passes postponement on hemp ban The House on Tuesday passed a short-term government funding bill that will buy the intoxicating hemp industry more time to fight off a looming crackdown on its products. © AP Photo/Markus Schreiber The continuing…
articles.body:
The House on Tuesday passed a short-term government funding bill that will buy the intoxicating hemp industry more time to fight off a looming crackdown on its products.

The continuing resolution, which funds the government through Dec. 11, passed the House on a 370-48 vote — with 19 Republicans and 29 Democrats voting in opposition. The Senate advanced the measure by a landslide last month, and it now heads to the desk of President Trump.

The measure postpones for a month a federal ban on most hemp-derived THC products , including gummies and beverages.

Hemp industry groups and their allies are touting Tuesday’s legislation as a significant win that will give them more time to convince lawmakers to regulate their products , rather than ban them.

“This extension gives us one additional month, and we intend to make every day count. We will continue working with lawmakers and stakeholders to advance a comprehensive federal framework that protects consumers, prevents youth access to intoxicating products, provides certainty for farmers and businesses, and preserves access to lawful hemp products,” the U.S. Hemp Roundtable said in an alert to members.

The delay excludes products containing cannabinoids “not capable of being naturally produced by a Cannabis sativa L. plant,” which will still be prohibited on Nov. 12. This likely includes illicit products from China.

However, cannabinoids like delta-8 THC, delta-10 THC and THCP , which are often synthetically derived from hemp, are also capable of being naturally produced by the plant, so they will be able to remain on shelves in gas stations, smoke shops and convenience stores until at least Dec. 11.

Supporters of keeping the original ban in place say they are trying to protect children from illicit products that are intentionally marketed to children. The products are labeled as hemp, but contain extremely high levels of synthetic THC, the psychedelic compound in marijuana responsible for a high.

The White House has made delaying or otherwise fixing the hemp ban a priority , making it likely that there will be a significant push to pass some kind of regulatory framework legislation this winter. Administration officials told lawmakers last month they will not seek another delay.

articles.title: 70 percent of young Americans not proud of where US is heading as nation: Poll
articles.summary: A majority of young Americans don’t have pride in the direction of their country, a newly released poll suggests. In a survey conducted by American University’s Sine Institute of Policy & Politics and published Tuesday, 70 percent of respondents — aged 18 to 34 — said they weren’t proud of “where America is heading as…
articles.body:
A majority of young Americans don’t have pride in the direction of their country, a newly released poll suggests.

In a survey conducted by American University’s Sine Institute of Policy & Politics and published Tuesday, 70 percent of respondents — aged 18 to 34 — said they weren’t proud of “where America is heading as a nation.” A similar number, 71 percent, said the same when asked about the state of the U.S. today.

The American University poll surveyed younger millennials and adult Generation Z members, which the study characterized as a demographic that has grown up amid significant political strife. The age group lived through prominent events ranging from the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks to the COVID-19 pandemic.

However, 59 percent of respondents also said they felt proud of the U.S. as it relates to “what [it] has been in the past.”

“Young people are navigating a rapidly changing America while carrying responsibilities that often extend far beyond themselves,” Molly O’Rourke, the institute’s senior advisor, said in a report of its findings. “Their views on the state of our country … tell an important story about this generation.”

The survey’s release comes amid growing doubt among the American public surrounding the Trump administration’s handling of U.S.’s war in Iran, rising living costs and immigration, among other concerns. It also marked the 250th anniversary of the U.S.’s founding.

Per a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, the president’s approval rating was sitting at 39.2 percent on Tuesday evening, with his disapproval rating at 57.20 percent.

American University ‘s poll took place from July 23 to Aug. 1 and featured 1,031 respondents.

But despite controversies involving Pressley's personal finances, her husband and racially charged remarks she's made, the "Squad member" will face no Republican candidate in the November general election.
